# Volume 3 — Chapter III Greeting and Farewell

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Wilfred Mott, Hugh Carrow, and Nell Harcourt departed from Brierley on the subsequent Monday morning. Nell had wished that the day would be fine. Isolde was scheduled to chauffeur her to the station, and the two desired that this drive, which would be their final one together for a while, might prove enjoyable. However, as Nell retired to bed on Sunday evening, the east wind was lamenting about Grey Shutters with a menacing prediction that came to pass when morning arrived. Upon waking, Nell discovered raindrops tapping against her windowpane and creating expanding circles on the gray face of the pond; fog concealed the hills and the sea, making the entire world appear dark and dismal. Nell put on her clothes in the gloomy gray twilight of dawn, since setting out early was required to make the connection for the boat train; she fought against tears that kept rising to her eyes regardless of her efforts. She was departing from the home she held so precious, and an inner feeling suggested that her departure was permanent, except for visits as a vacation retreat. Circumstances would never return to what they had been; returning for holidays would not constitute residing there. And oh, how cherished and adored every single detail was—that small white porch room, dedicated to the daydreams of her youth, the ancient Frost Maiden by the window, the stream down in the hollow, the Nymph’s Well, the Haunted Woods, and Linger Lane—every one of the countless beloved places where recollections of former years lingered. Was it possible for her to ever experience true happiness in any other place?
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0000 }

Morning meal at Grey Shutters on that day was quite a gloomy affair. Likely for the initial time in his existence, Robin was unable to consume food, instead weeping openly above his porridge. Except for Lucy, who consumed her portion with ease, no one else appeared to possess much of a desire to eat. Lucy resembled the famed and highly sensible Charlotte, who “went on cutting bread and butter” as the corpse of her frantic suitor was borne by on a shutter, being among those lucky individuals whom almost nothing upsets. A lot was required to disturb the calm of Lucy, even at the age of eight. Naturally, she felt regret over the departure of Nell, yet did that justify not enjoying a poached egg on toast? It certainly did not. Consequently, observing that Robin was incapable of consuming his own, Lucy consumed it in his place.
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0001 }

Punctually at the appointed hour Isolde arrived with horse and buggy, her flushed countenance shining over her raincoat. At that point, the farewells somehow needed to be spoken. Entering from her quarters, Mrs. Sowerby warmly hugged Nell and cautioned her to take care of her health, no matter what happened. Thirza, abrupt and without tears, lightly kissed Nell’s cheek and remarked she presumed they would receive word from her once she was established. An onlooker without intimate knowledge might have assumed that Nell’s departure was of small consequence to her—except if that onlooker had chanced to catch a clear glimpse into her eyes. Lucy gave Nell a stiff kiss and managed to produce two neat, small tears; yet Robin, who had been weeping on the back porch step from the moment they left the table, declined to bid farewell whatsoever. Observing Nell approach him, he leaped up, rushed up the rear staircase, and concealed himself inside a clothes closet, refusing to emerge. The last noises Nell caught as she departed Grey Shutters were his deadened cries.
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0002 }

Downpours fell unceasingly throughout the journey to Alder River, the depot they were required to travel to because the feeder line train coming from Delford failed to link up with the boat train. Upon their arrival, Wilfred and Hugh stood waiting on the station platform while the train emitted its whistle. Nell barely managed to obtain her ticket and trunk check, bid a hasty goodbye to Isolde, and rush onto the train. She longed to return to Brierley alongside Isolde, feeling certain that homesickness would be her death. Furthermore, if merely that dreary rain would cease cascading down as though all creation grieved for lost summer and gone delights! Not even Hugh’s presence offered her solace, because Wilfred Mott accompanied them as well, and Sloanishness was bearable exclusively during pleasant weather. In the rain, it was utterly unendurable.
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0003 }

Yet conditions improved once the vessel navigated away from the harbor at Port Marlow. Rain stopped falling, and through openings in the cloud cover, the sun started breaking through in golden flashes here and there, polishing the dull sea with a reddish-metallic glow, and illuminating the vapors draping the red coasts of the Island with flashes of gold that promised a pleasant day would come after all. Furthermore, Wilfred Mott was quickly afflicted by such intense seasickness that he was forced to head down into the cabin, leaving Nell and Hugh by themselves on the deck.
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0004 }

“It is a great relief to me that every Mott becomes seasick the moment they are on the water,” Nell reflected without pity. “If Wilfred were beside me feigning a sentimental gaze at it, I know I would be unable to cast my final glance upon the ‘ould sod.’”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0005 }

“Well, we’re leaving,” Hugh stated without emotion.
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0006 }

“Indeed, Byron’s ‘Childe Harold’ comes to mind for me—except the land I am observing is not actually my ‘native shore’,” Nell remarked, her gray eyes blinking rapidly. “I guess Nova Scotia holds that title. Nevertheless, the place a person cherishes most constitutes their true native shore, and for my part, that is dear old P.E.I. That I haven't spent my entire life here seems unbelievable. A nightmare is what those initial eleven years prior to my arrival feel like. Seven years have passed since I made the passage aboard this vessel—on the same night Mrs. Tranter transported me from Hopetown. I picture my former self, clad in that hideous old wincey garment and washed-out sailor hat, investigating the decks and cabins with blissful wonder. The evening was lovely; and the way those red shores of the Island shone under the sun was remarkable. At present, I am making the strait crossing once more. Oh, Hugh, my sincere wish is that Wexcombe and Portmaris prove pleasing to me, though my certainty is that they won't!”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0007 }

“Nell, where has the whole of your philosophy vanished to?”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0008 }

“A massive, overwhelming surge of solitude and longing for home covers everything completely. For three years I have yearned to travel to Wexcombe—and my journey is happening now—and I desire not to go! Do not worry! Once I have simply one thorough cry, my cheerful and philosophical nature will return. I need to experience that, ‘as a went’—and my wait must continue until I reach my boardinghouse bed this evening, wherever that might be, before I am able to indulge in it. At that point Nell will return to her true self. I ponder whether Robin has emerged from the closet at this time.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0009 }

When their train arrived in Portmaris at nine o'clock that evening, they stepped into the crowded station's harsh blue-white illumination. Nell experienced a sense of terrible confusion, yet shortly afterward, Honora Hollis, who had arrived in Portmaris the previous Saturday, grabbed hold of her.
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0010 }

“You have arrived, my love! I assume you are just as exhausted as I was upon my arrival Saturday night.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0011 }

“Exhausted! Honora, avoid speaking about that. I am exhausted, alongside being naive, unsophisticated, and merely roughly a decade of age. For mercy's sake, escort your miserable, exhausted friend to a spot where it is possible for her to listen to her own thoughts.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0012 }

“I will escort you straight to our boardinghouse. My cab is waiting just outside.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0013 }

“Having you present is a true blessing, Sukey. Had you not been, I believe I would merely collapse upon my luggage, right this moment, and shed sorrowful tears. How reassuring a single recognizable countenance proves to be amidst a roaring sea of unknown people!”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0014 }

“Does that happen to be Hugh Carrow over there, Nell? The way he has matured throughout this last year is remarkable! During my time teaching in Delford, he was merely a schoolboy. Naturally, that other person is Wilfred Mott. No change has come over him—none was possible! His appearance was identical to that at his birth, and at eighty years old he will retain that very same look. Head this direction, dear. Our arrival home will take just twenty minutes.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0015 }

“Home!” Nell groaned. “You mean we’ll be located in a terrible boardinghouse, situated in a hall bedroom that is even more terrible, facing a gloomy back yard.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0016 }

“This isn't a dreadful lodging, Nell-girl. Our cab has arrived. Get inside—our trunk will be retrieved by the cabbie. Ah, yes, regarding the lodging—it is truly quite a fine establishment for what it is, which you will acknowledge by tomorrow morning after a restful night converts your sadness to cheerful optimism. It consists of a large, aged, gray stone dwelling located on St. John Street, situated merely a pleasant short walk away from Wexcombe. High society used to consider it their ‘residence’, yet style has departed from St. John Street, leaving its structures to merely daydream about finer times. Their size is so grand that the occupants must accept lodgers simply to occupy the space. In any case, that represents the explanation our hostesses are extremely eager to emphasize to us. They are wonderful, Nell—I am referring to our hostesses.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0017 }

“What is their count?”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0018 }

“Two. Miss Hannah Harvey together with Miss Ada Harvey. Their births as twins occurred approximately fifty years back.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0019 }

“It appears I am unable to escape twins,” Nell said with a smile. “They face me everywhere I travel.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0020 }

“Oh, dear, they are not twins any longer. They ceased to be twins once they turned thirty. Miss Hannah has aged, though not very gracefully, whereas Miss Ada has remained thirty, with even less grace. Whether Miss Hannah is capable of smiling or not is unknown to me; I have not yet seen her do so, but Miss Ada wears a constant smile, which is far worse. Even so, they are pleasant, good-hearted people who host two boarders annually because Miss Hannah’s thrifty nature refuses to allow room space to be 'wasted'—it is not out of necessity or obligation, a fact Miss Ada has informed me of seven times since Saturday evening. Regarding our quarters, I confess they are hall bedrooms, and my own faces the back yard. Yours is situated at the front, overlooking Old St. John’s graveyard, located directly across the street.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0021 }

“That seems horrific,” shuddered Nell. “I believe I’d prefer looking out over the back yard.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0022 }

“Indeed, you would not. Just wait and observe. Old St. John’s is a lovely location. Having functioned as a burial ground for so long, it no longer serves that purpose and has transformed into one of the attractions of Portmaris. Yesterday, I traversed the entire grounds for a recreational outing. A large stone wall together with a line of massive trees encircles it completely, and lines of trees run all through its interior, alongside the strangest old gravestones featuring the strangest and most charming epitaphs. You will head there to study, Nell, mark my words. Naturally, no one receives a burial there anymore. However, several years ago, a striking monument was erected to honor Nova Scotian soldiers who perished during the Crimean War. Located directly across from the entry gates, it offers ‘scope for imagination’, as you were accustomed to saying. At long last, your trunk has arrived—and the boys are approaching to bid us good night. Is it truly necessary for me to shake hands with Wilfred Mott, Nell? The feeling of his hands is perpetually so cold and fish-like. We ought to invite them to visit from time to time. Miss Hannah solemnly informed me that ‘young gentlemen callers’ were permitted two nights a week, provided their departure occurred at a sensible time; while Miss Ada, with a smile, requested that I ensure they refrained from sitting on her lovely cushions. I pledged to manage that; though goodness knows what other seating exists for them, short of sitting on the floor, because cushions rest upon every surface. Miss Ada has even placed an ornate Battenburg one atop the piano.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0023 }

By this time, Nell was laughing. Her spirits were cheered, as intended, by the lively talk of Honora; for the moment, her longing for home disappeared, and it failed to come back at maximum strength even when she ultimately was by herself in her small bedroom. Going to her window, she gazed outside. Shadowy and peaceful was the street underneath. On the opposite side, over the trees in Old St. John’s, the moon shone right behind the huge, dark head of the lion situated on the monument. Nell pondered whether her departure from Grey Shutters had occurred only that morning. She experienced that feeling of a lengthy duration passing which a single day filled with movement and new experiences creates.
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0024 }

“I guess that exact moon is shining on Grey Shutters right now,” she pondered. “However I will not dwell on it—down that path lies homesickness. I am not even going to indulge in my good cry. I will delay that until a more fitting time, and for now I will go peacefully and reasonably to bed and to sleep.”
{: #nw-v03-c03-p0025 }
